item.title: Keeping Score Is a Relationship Killer
item.description:
Relationships

Keeping Score Is a Relationship Killer

Why couples can lose their sense of being teammates.

Posted June 8, 2026

Key points
  • Exhaustion can turn relationships into cycles of emotional scorekeeping.
  • Resentment grows when partners stop feeling recognized and appreciated.
  • Repair strengthens relationships when couples shift from competition back toward collaboration.
Source: peopleimages12 / 123rf.com

Leah and Omar had always thought of themselves as a strong team. Leah, a pediatric nurse, worked long shifts at the hospital. Omar, a freelance videographer, balanced unpredictable hours, client deadlines, and the pressure of inconsistent income. Together, they coordinated demanding schedules while raising their two young children.

Early in their relationship, their differences complemented each other well. Leah brought structure and consistency. Omar brought flexibility, humor, and creativity. Both admired how hard the other worked and often described themselves as partners who could adapt to almost anything together.

After welcoming twins, life demanded even more of them. They felt constantly exhausted, and the quality time they once enjoyed together gradually disappeared. Although neither questioned the other’s love or commitment, both began feeling overextended and increasingly disconnected from one another.

Crash: When Exhaustion Turns Into Scorekeeping

The tension did not begin with one major argument. Instead, it developed slowly through dozens of small interactions.

Leah became irritated when she came home after difficult shifts and found unfinished chores waiting for her. When she pointed out tasks Omar had missed, he often became defensive and responded with criticism of his own. On one occasion, Omar came home frustrated that an errand he assumed had been handled was still unfinished.

This pattern repeated itself over and over. Both partners began mentally tracking what the other had failed to do while overlooking everything the other was contributing. Gradually, resentment began replacing appreciation.

“I already did that.”

“I guess you don’t think I can handle it.”

“Must be nice.”

“You don’t think I’m tired too?”

Comments like these became increasingly common. The relationship began feeling less like a partnership and more like a competition. Leah and Omar both felt that their efforts were only noticed when something went wrong.

What made the situation particularly painful was that both genuinely believed they were trying hard. Both felt exhausted. Both felt criticized. Both felt underappreciated.

In Love. Crash. Rebuild., we describe how rupture can develop when stress narrows attention and interferes with the reciprocity that helps relationships feel balanced and supportive. Partners can become so focused on their own exhaustion and unmet needs that they gradually lose sight of each other’s effort, vulnerability, and goodwill.

Rebuild: Using PACER to Interrupt the Scorekeeping Cycle

Pause

The shift began after a relatively minor disagreement escalated far beyond the original issue. In the middle of the argument, Leah and Omar realized they were no longer fighting about chores or schedules. They were fighting about resentment, rejection, and a growing sense of not being appreciated by one another.

Pause helped them step back from the immediate conflict. They came to understand that their conversations had become organized around mistakes, unfinished tasks, and defending their own efforts rather than understanding each other’s experience.

Accountability

Leah acknowledged that she had become so focused on what remained unfinished that she rarely communicated appreciation for what Omar was doing well. As resentment grew, she became more critical and less collaborative, even when she knew Omar was overwhelmed, too.

Omar acknowledged that he often minimized Leah’s exhaustion because he felt consumed by his own stress about work, finances, and parenting. Rather than expressing his vulnerability directly, he often responded with defensiveness, sarcasm, or criticism.

Neither partner intended to create emotional distance. Both had become trapped in cycles of exhaustion and self-protection that gradually transformed teamwork into competition.

Collaboration

As their conversations became more open and honest, Leah and Omar began discussing the invisible burdens each had been carrying privately. Instead of debating who worked harder, they focused on recognizing how much each was contributing to the family.

Leah explained that constantly tracking unfinished responsibilities left her feeling mentally overloaded and emotionally alone. Omar explained that he also felt isolated when he focused primarily on Leah’s mistakes rather than her efforts. Both realized they had become far more aware of what was missing than what was working.

Collaboration shifted their interactions away from criticism and scorekeeping and toward rebuilding mutual understanding and appreciation.

Experiment

They began having more intentional conversations about workload, appreciation, and expectations. Leah practiced expressing gratitude more directly when Omar’s efforts helped her feel supported. Omar practiced acknowledging Leah’s contributions before frustration had a chance to build.

Both also worked on becoming more empathetic toward each other’s daily experiences. Instead of focusing on what remained undone, they practiced recognizing what had already been accomplished. Small comments, such as “We both worked hard today,” helped interrupt the cycle of criticism and defensiveness.

Reset

Over time, the emotional distance between them began to shrink. Stress and conflict did not disappear, but the relationship gradually stopped feeling like a competition that left both partners isolated and alone.

Some weeks, one partner still carried more than the other. What changed was their ability to discuss those imbalances collaboratively and empathetically without turning them into evidence of failure or rejection.

Their relationship began feeling more like a partnership again.

Why This Matters

Stress and exhaustion can quietly transform relationships into painful competitions. Partners begin tracking each other’s failures and defending their own contributions while losing sight of each other’s efforts, limitations, and humanity.

In Leah and Omar’s case, both partners felt exhausted, resentful, and underappreciated. Neither intended to create distance, yet both became trapped in a cycle that reinforced it.

The PACER process helps couples slow these patterns down so that accountability, appreciation, and collaboration become possible again.

item.title: 2 Necessary Lies That Every Relationship Needs
item.description:
Relationships

2 Necessary Lies That Every Relationship Needs

Why honesty isn't always the best policy when it comes to love.

Posted June 8, 2026

Source: Getty Images / Unsplash

Honesty and transparency are the gold standard of healthy relationships for good reason, as trust depends on them. Without a basic expectation of truthfulness, a relationship will quickly become unstable. Partners will start to second-guess each other’s intentions and commitment.

Absolutes rarely govern human relationships; with every reasonable rule comes an equally reasonable exception. This means that, in practice, even the healthiest couples will sometimes bend the truth. And interestingly, research suggests that some forms of dishonesty and certain kinds of lies may actually serve an important relational purpose.

This is because, while brutal honesty sounds virtuous in theory, in many scenarios, relentless truth-telling is more likely to damage closeness than strengthen it. As such, a loving relationship will demand awareness that, sometimes, not every truth needs to be delivered in its rawest form.

Here are two “necessary lies” that many healthy relationships depend on, according to psychological research.

1. Prosocial Lies

One of the most common forms of dishonesty in romantic relationships is the prosocial lie—a lie that, in the grand scheme of things, is ultimately positive; it promotes social acceptance and cohesion.

In a 2026 study published in The Journal of Social Psychology, researchers explored how people in romantic relationships feel about hearing prosocial lies from their partner. The authors of the study found that, although honesty remains important overall, many individuals actually preferred comforting or reassuring dishonesty over the harsh truth in certain situations. This was especially true for participants who felt that their relationship was strained.

Interestingly, researchers also found that people with lower relationship satisfaction were more likely to prefer prosocial lies. Partly, this is because they perceived blunt truths as emotionally harmful. This shows that when a relationship is in a vulnerable state, emotional cushioning proves especially valuable.

This makes intuitive sense, as relationships are not merely systems of information exchange. Partners must constantly regulate one another’s sense of security and confidence, and, once in a while, that means softening reality.

Take “compliment buffering,” for example. Imagine your partner has spent hours cooking an elaborate dinner specially for you. The meal turns out fine—it’s not terrible, but it’s not particularly memorable either. A fully transparent response might sound like, “Honestly, it was a little bland.” Is this answer technically truthful? Yes. Is it helpful? Probably not.

In many cases, saying, “That was delicious! Thank you for putting so much effort into spoiling me,” would serve the relationship much better than the truth. Because in this scenario, the goal isn’t for you to start a career as a food critic; your partner likely isn’t asking you solely for an objective evaluation of the food. They are asking whether their efforts and affection have landed as well as they hoped.

Of course, prosocial lies can become unhealthy when they consistently serve to conceal major incompatibilities or prevent honest communication. For instance, telling your partner that you love a lifestyle that secretly makes you miserable is not kindness; that’s just avoiding a necessary conversation.

But in moderation, these small acts of emotional buffering play an important, invisible role in a relationship’s smooth function. They represent a core tenet that should be prioritized in any loving relationship: that feelings matter more than either partner’s need to be technically correct.

2. Protective Lies

Another category of “necessary” dishonesty involves “protective lies”: lies told in the hopes of shielding partners from unnecessary emotional harm.

In a 2025 study published in Personal Relationships, researchers examined dishonesty in romantic relationships and found that people commonly described their lies as protective. These lies typically fell into one of two categories: partner-protective or self-protective lies.

While the latter forms of lie largely function by making partners feel good, these lies serve to prevent partners from feeling bad. These are the kinds of deceptions that revolve around emotional regulation, rather than manipulation. They help couples avoid turning every fleeting irritation, insecurity, or comparison into a relationship-threatening discussion.

For instance, many partners have small gripes or annoyances with habits that are annoying at worst, but far from an outright red flag—like a partner who chews somewhat loudly, leaves cabinet doors open, or hums constantly while working. If you were to highlight every one of these minor inconveniences with complete honesty, then daily life would soon become emotionally exhausting.

Instead, most couples will opt for selective silence. They smooth over these small irritations because they’ve learned firsthand that love requires a certain degree of patience and tolerance. Constant correction only makes for an atmosphere of surveillance and nitpickiness. These lies preserve dignity. If you were to recall all of their embarrassing or upsetting moments with perfect accuracy every time, they’d likely feel more exposed than supported.

And most notably, protective lies will even appear in romance itself. For example, you might have told your partner, “I’ve never felt this way before,” even though you’ve experienced deep love in a past relationship. While, strictly speaking, the statement may not be fully true, emotionally, it still reflects something real: your desire to communicate just how singular and meaningful this relationship is to you.

Romantic bonds thrive partly because couples create a shared narrative of uniqueness around their connection—something most intelligent people know and understand on an internal level. You wouldn’t tell your partner, “Actually, this feels somewhat comparable to my relationship three years ago.” While this might be a more accurate statement, it also totally undermines the relationship itself.

It’s worth emphasizing that protective lies differ vastly from deception. Deception is used to evade responsibility, manipulate a partner, or conceal betrayal. Hiding infidelity, financial dishonesty, or chronic disrespect are not, by any stretch of the imagination, “necessary lies.” Healthy protective lies are typically temporary and emotionally motivated rather than self-serving. They mitigate friction without distorting reality in a way that fundamentally alters consent or trust.

Ultimately, a successful relationship demands more than just honesty alone. Kindness, restraint, tact, and emotional intelligence will, on the odd occasion, take priority over full transparency. Because, sometimes, preserving intimacy means recognizing that being loving and being completely unfiltered are not always the same thing.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.

item.title: Developing Specialty Skills in Clinical Aviation Psychology
item.description:
Career

Developing Specialty Skills in Clinical Aviation Psychology

Ways to obtain education and training in clinical aviation psychology.

Posted June 8, 2026

Key points
  • Formal training in clinical aviation psychology is scarce but essential for public safety.
  • FAA and HIMS offer specialized training and guidelines for psychologists assessing flight personnel.
  • Experiential learning, like flying lessons and listening to air traffic control, boosts cultural competence.

Psychologists and other mental health professionals are key to assessing and treating our aviation populations. Both civilian and military flight crews, air traffic controllers, unmanned aerial systems operators, and pilots must meet medical and mental health requirements to ensure public safety. Providing services to this population requires specialized skills and knowledge to make simultaneous decisions in the context of the individual as well as public safety. Consequently, these evaluations are high stakes for all involved.

Despite the importance, there are few avenues to obtain formal education and training in what is interchangeably termed clinical aviation psychology, aeromedical psychology, and aerospace psychology. This post provides suggestions to gain professional and cultural competence in the absence of a robust training pipeline in this specialty area.

Psychological assessment of flight personnel requires advanced skills.
Source: Clker-Free-Vector-Images / Pixabay

Learn About Aviation

There are excellent aviation museums around the country, as well as routine air shows provided by a number of organizations. These types of learning opportunities are a good starting point to gain exposure to the occupational demands of flight as well as the psychology of flight personnel.

Take a Flying Lesson

One familiarization flight at the controls of an aircraft is not sufficient to gain cultural competence in working with the aviation population. However, it does provide a glimpse into the cognitive load, communication skills, decision-making, and other skills needed by flight personnel. Additionally, it puts you in a position in which your awareness of your dependence on the pilot for your own personal safety is more profound than when flying as a passenger on a commercial flight. And, contextually, every evaluation that you perform or recommendation that you make that someone is ready to start or return to flying is about people’s safety.

Listen to Air Traffic Control

Listening to air traffic control communications also provides a window into the cognitive and emotional functioning necessary for flight duties. Controllers, especially in busy airspace, are juggling multiple aircraft simultaneously in a high-stakes situation, and pilots must constantly adapt to the shifting demands of the airspace and the direction of the controllers. LiveATC allows you to listen to the radio traffic of many airports and gain an appreciation for the duties, cognitive load, and emotional regulation involved.

Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Training and Qualification

The FAA website provides valuable information for psychologists who are performing evaluations of flight personnel, and it is recommended that any psychologist assessing or treating this population become familiar with these online guides and resources. The FAA maintains requirements for clinical psychologists and neuropsychologists performing specific evaluations of pilots and air traffic control specialists (ATCS) and routinely provides training for psychologists to meet these requirements. These trainings include:

  • Tier 2 training: The Tier 2 program provides community psychologists with the training needed to assess ATCS applicants who require additional evaluation following their Tier 1 screening (an occupationally mandated pre-employment screening). Tier 2 assessments are in-person psychological evaluations with stringent requirements such that they can be used by the FAA to make risk management decisions regarding applicants.
  • HIMS training: The Human Intervention Motivational Study (HIMS) is not an FAA program, but is a collaborative program of which the FAA is a partner. It is designed to support pilots with a substance or mental health diagnosis. There are two levels of HIMS training for psychologists and neuropsychologists: the Basic Conference and the Advanced Conference. The Basic Conference provides the necessary education and training for participation in the HIMS program, to include the requirements for the mandated psychological evaluations. The Advanced Conference builds upon the basic training and includes such topics as complex case reviews.
  • Aerospace Behavioral Health Seminar: The FAA provides an Aerospace Behavioral Health Seminar annually, which covers a variety of topics relevant to the assessment of flight personnel. Topics include relevant policy and regulations, assessment, personality factors, report writing, ethics, psychotropic medications, and case examples. The Tier 2 training mentioned above is provided as a part of this seminar.

These trainings are required in most cases every three years for psychologists to maintain their status as HIMS/Aviation Psychologists through the FAA.

Read Relevant Professional Literature

There are journals devoted to medical topics in aviation, and, given its public health and safety significance, many non-aviation-specific journals publish relevant articles. Two journals that are focused on aeromedical topics are Aerospace Medicine and Human Performance and the International Journal of Aerospace Psychology. Additionally, aviation topics are covered in this blog series. Currently available topics are: airsickness in flight personnel, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, flight personnel and psychiatric medication, call signs, and compartmentalization.

Mental Health Conference Attendance

Although there are few formal training opportunities outside of the FAA, there has been a systematic increase in relevant conference content across the mental health fields broadly. Finding these sessions requires some diligence, but there are often one or more devoted to aviation at the conferences of large professional mental health organizations. When planning your conference attendance, include these sessions.

Military Training

For those psychologists serving in the military, the Air Force, Army, and Navy all have formal aeromedical psychology training courses. Military aeromedical training has been shown to improve decision-making by psychologists and psychiatrists, significantly improving outcomes for both individuals and the organization. For individuals, flight personnel are twice as likely to be able to continue flying (i.e., obtain waivers), and for the organization, trained aeromedical professionals make more accurate risk decisions and better streamline the aeromedical decision process, eliminating unnecessary delays that keep flyers out of their aircraft and controllers out of the tower.

Assessing and treating high-risk populations requires an advanced standard of professional and cultural competence. It is up to each individual psychologist performing assessment and treatment of the aviation population to ensure this competence, in an environment where formal training can be hard to come by. Fortunately, it does appear that training opportunities are increasing, though challenges remain and diligence in finding opportunities for yourself continues to be necessary.

item.title: When Irritability Isn't "Just a Phase"
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

When Irritability Isn't "Just a Phase"

Understanding disruptive mood dysregulation disorder.

Posted June 8, 2026

Key points
  • DMDD is a mental health condition characterized by chronic irritability and severe emotional outbursts.
  • Evidence-based diagnostic criteria helps clinicians differentiate DMDD from other conditions.
  • Well-established therapeutic approaches can significantly improve emotional regulation and family functioning.

Most parents expect occasional meltdowns, mood swings, and emotional outbursts. Childhood is, after all, a time of learning how to navigate big feelings. But what happens when anger seems to dominate a child's daily experience? What if irritability becomes the norm rather than the exception?

For some children, chronic irritability and explosive emotional reactions may point to a condition called disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (DMDD).

DMDD is a relatively new diagnosis, introduced in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) in 2013. Its creation addressed an important problem in child psychiatry: many children with severe irritability and frequent temper outbursts were being diagnosed with pediatric bipolar disorder, even though their symptoms didn't truly fit that condition.

Researchers recognized that these children were experiencing something different. Rather than cycling between extreme highs and lows, they lived in a near-constant state of irritability punctuated by intense emotional explosions. DMDD was created to better describe and understand this pattern.

In essence, children with DMDD experience frequent, severe temper outbursts that are significantly out of proportion to the situation. These outbursts may be:

  • Verbal: yelling, screaming, or cursing.
  • Behavioral: hitting, kicking, flailing around on the floor, damage to property.
  • Both verbal and behavioral.
  • The outbursts occur regularly, typically three or more times per week.

What makes DMDD distinct, however, isn't just the tantrums. Between outbursts, these children remain persistently irritable or angry most of the day, nearly every day. Parents often describe them as being "on edge," easily annoyed, or chronically unhappy.

DMDD is typically diagnosed between 6 and 18 years of age. To meet diagnostic criteria:

  • Symptoms must persist for at least a year.
  • Symptoms must occur across multiple settings, such as home, school, or interactions with peers.
  • Symptoms must begin before age 10.

The important takeaway is this: if your school-age child seems angry, frustrated, or irritated most of the time and frequently has over-the-top emotional reactions to minor irritations, it may be worth discussing DMDD with a qualified mental health professional.

Looking Beyond the Behavior

One of the biggest mistakes adults make is focusing solely on the behavior itself.

When a child is yelling, throwing things, or refusing to cooperate, it's easy to become consumed with stopping the behavior. But behavior is communication. Beneath the outburst is often a child struggling with emotional regulation skills they have not yet developed.

Children with DMDD aren't choosing to feel irritable. They aren't waking up each morning with the intention to make life difficult for their parents or teachers. Their nervous systems are often operating in a state of heightened emotional reactivity, making everyday frustrations feel overwhelming.

This perspective doesn't excuse inappropriate behavior, but it does guide us toward more effective interventions.

Therapy as a First-Line Treatment

The good news is that effective treatments are available. Therapy is often one of the first recommendations and can be highly effective when tailored to a child's specific challenges.

  • Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT): helps children identify thoughts, emotions, and behaviors while developing healthier coping strategies. It teaches emotional regulation, problem-solving, and resilience skills that can reduce the intensity of emotional reactions.
  • Parent management training (PMT): focuses on helping parents respond more effectively to challenging behaviors. Parents learn strategies that reduce unintentional reinforcement of disruptive behaviors while strengthening connection and cooperation.
  • Dialectical behavior therapy for children (DBT-C): emphasizes emotional regulation, distress tolerance, mindfulness, and interpersonal effectiveness. For children whose emotions quickly escalate, these skills can be transformative.

There is also a therapy that I wish I had learned about much earlier in my career: eye movement desensitization and reprocessing, or EMDR. Originally developed to treat trauma, EMDR uses specific patterns of eye movement while an individual recalls distressing experiences. Research suggests that this process helps the brain reprocess traumatic memories, reducing their emotional intensity and allowing healthier adaptive beliefs to emerge.

While EMDR is most associated with trauma treatment, its applications continue to expand. For some children whose emotional dysregulation is connected to adverse experiences, it can be an important part of a comprehensive treatment plan.

When Medication May Help

Medication is another treatment option that may be appropriate for some children, particularly when therapy alone isn't providing enough relief. One commonly prescribed class of medications for children and adolescents with DMDD are selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs).

SSRIs work by increasing the availability of serotonin, a neurotransmitter involved in regulating mood, anxiety, and emotional well-being. By blocking serotonin reuptake, these medications allow more serotonin to remain available in the brain.

Like any medication, SSRIs have potential side effects. Common ones include nausea, headaches, sleep disturbances, and changes in appetite. Some children may initially experience increased irritability or restlessness during the first few weeks of treatment.

Because of this, close monitoring is essential whenever a child begins an SSRI. Families should maintain open communication with their prescribing clinician and report any concerning changes promptly.

However, SSRIs can dramatically improve mood, decrease irritability, and minimize the impact of temper tantrums. Yet the decision to start medication must be individually based, and include recommendations from appropriate mental health providers, parents, and sometimes even the patients themselves.

The Bottom Line

Parenting a child with chronic irritability and emotional outbursts can be exhausting. It can also feel isolating, especially when others assume your child simply needs more discipline or better behavior.

But children with DMDD aren't choosing their struggles. They are often working incredibly hard to manage emotions that feel overwhelming and difficult to control. They simply do not have the skills or resources to do so.

The encouraging news is that with appropriate support, effective therapy, and, when indicated, medication, these children can learn the skills needed to regulate their emotions more successfully.

As parents, our role isn't to punish emotional struggles away. It's to understand what's driving them and help our children build the tools they need to thrive.

Sometimes what looks like defiance is actually distress—and recognizing the difference can change everything.

item.title: How Friendship Transformed Kant’s Life
item.description:
Friends

How Friendship Transformed Kant’s Life

Kant’s philosophy of friendship, and how it differed from Aristotle’s.

Posted June 8, 2026

Key points
  • Kant’s famous daily routine was inspired by his closest friend, Joseph Green.
  • Kant discussed every single sentence of the Critique of Pure Reason with Green.
  • After Green died, Kant became more housebound, and wrote down his thoughts on friendship.
Kant at the age of 44, by Johann Gottlieb Becker.
Source: Wikimedia Commons/Johann Gottlieb Becker/Public Domain.

In his youth and middle age, the sharply dressed Immanuel Kant (1724-1804) moved in Königsberg’s most refined circles and often stayed out into the small hours. In this period, his student Johann Gottfriend Herder described him as “the most urbane fellow in the world.”

But when Kant turned forty, he underwent a midlife transformation. He quite literally sobered up, abandoning carefree carousing for the disciplined life of the mind. This profound change owed to the early death of a close friend, the dissolute Johann Daniel Funk, together with the making of a new friend, the English merchant Joseph Green, who lived by the clock.

Kant essentially adopted Green’s modus vivendi.

Kant’s Daily Routine, and How It Helped Him

For the rest of his productive life, Kant employed a retired solder, Martin Lampe, to wake him up at precisely five-to-five every morning. Lampe would stride into his master’s bedroom and cry out, “Herr Professor, the time is come!" Or in German, Herr Professor, es ist Zeit!

Kant worked at his desk in his nightclothes until his lectures began at seven. At eleven, he would change back into nightclothes and return to his desk. The working day effectively ended at one, when he would take lunch in company in a public inn or restaurant. Lunch would end at three with a round of manufactured jokes—in the belief that laughter was good for digestion and broader health.

At three, after lunch, Kant would take his daily constitutional around Königsberg. He would walk alone, from fear that outdoor conversation would lead him to breathe through the mouth. He often wound up at Green’s, with whom he liked to discuss Hume and Rousseau. It is said that the housewives of Königsberg would set their timepieces by the time—seven sharp—at which he left Green’s house.

By automating trivial daily decisions, Kant’s rigid daily routine freed his mind to focus purely on philosophy. It's because of Kant that I have six of the same shirt.

Kant’s Jokes and Philosophy of Laughter

What kind of jokes did Kant tell after lunch? Some of his jokes have come down to us in his writing. For instance: A man tried to arrange a solemn funeral for a rich relative, but failed in the task: “The more I paid my mourners, the merrier they looked.” A merchant sailed back from India with his fortune, but, in a violent storm, had to throw all his cargo overboard. This upset him so much that his wig turned grey overnight.

Laughter, Kant thought, “is an affect resulting from the sudden transformation of a heightened expectation into nothing.” The mind is deceived into tensing up, but with the deception revealed suddenly relaxes, leading to laughter, which mimics the motions of the mind and is extremely health-giving. Kant never laughed at his own jokes, but always kept a straight face.

In The Critique of Pure Judgement (1790), Kant quoted Voltaire in saying that Heaven had given us two comforts against life’s hardships, hope and sleep—before suggesting that Voltaire “could have added laughter.”

The Death of Joseph Green

In 1786, Joseph Green died, deeply affecting Kant, who, thereafter, became a lot more housebound.

After a suitable period of mourning, Kant recruited a female cook and began hosting protracted lunches aimed at stimulating the play of thoughts. To this end, he gathered guests from diverse backgrounds and perspectives, believing that the ideal number of guests lay somewhere in between that of the Graces and the Muses (three and nine). All topics great and small were on the table. Philosophy was allowed but not dogmatism, for fear that it would interrupt the convivial flow of ideas.

As well as wine (another of God's comforts), Kant had a taste for Königsberger Klopse (meatballs in a creamy white sauce with capers), Teltow turnips (an heirloom turnip from the Berlin-Brandenburg region), roast beef, cod, and, as a condiment for the above, English mustard, which he mixed himself in the belief that his mix protected against senescence.

Kant’s Philosophy of Friendship

Joseph Green was the closest friend that Kant ever had. Green had inspired Kant’s routine, and became his philosophical sounding board. Kant allegedly discussed every single sentence of the Critique of Pure Reason with Green before publishing it in 1781.

In the Metaphysics of Morals (1797), Kant ended his discussion of character traits just like, in the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle ended his discussion of the same: with an analysis of friendship.

In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle made much of the idea of “perfect friendship”, which, he thought, is only possible between men of reason and virtue. He famously described a perfect friend as “another self”—later paraphrased by Diogenes Laertius as “a single soul dwelling in two bodies.”

Kant deemed “perfect friendship” an ideal that in practice cannot be attained. But in striving for it, we might nonetheless arrive at “moral friendship,” in which two persons feel able to disclose their secret thoughts and feelings to each other. Moral friendship requires a savant mélange of love and respect, love for bringing two people together, and respect for not driving them apart by infringing upon their dignity and autonomy.

From his own experience, Kant came to believe that most people cannot develop their true character until middle age, when they might undergo a “rebirth”. At twenty, we are no more than the product of our upbringing and environment. At thirty, we are still reliant on the judgement and approval of others. Only at forty are we confident enough (or perhaps tired enough) to become who we truly are.

Neel Burton is the author of the newly published The German Greeks: German Philosophy and the German Philosophers.

item.title: We Become What We Attend To
item.description:
Attention

We Become What We Attend To

How attention shapes the bridge between consciousness and subconsciousness.

Posted June 8, 2026

Key points
  • Attention is key to unlocking the space between the conscious and subconscious.
  • The brain receives vastly more information than consciousness can process. Attention acts as a filter.
  • Attention has parts that are under volitional control and parts that are beyond our control.

“I am more forgetful these days. Is this normal for old age or am I getting dementia?“

This is one of the most common questions I get asked as a neurologist. There is no easy way to answer this question—it is our job to do a whole evaluation, a bit of detective work to figure this out, but in broad terms, there are two reasons we may not remember something. One is a true problem with encoding or storing memory. The other is an attention problem: the information never fully entered the system in the first place.

If you focus and try to remember, and still cannot remember, this may suggest a true memory problem.

But much of what people describe as "memory problems" are actually attention problems.

What Is Attention?

The word “attention” is used ubiquitously: “attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)," "pay attention,” or "our attention span is getting shorter in this era of social media." But in neuroscience, compared to a more concrete mental faculty like language, memory, motor control, or vision, how attention works is still not fully understood.

Having said that, “attention” may be the key to unlock the space between consciousness and the subconscious. It is a switch, a filter, and perhaps one of the most powerful tools we have for shaping our inner life.

Gorilla Suit on the Basketball Court

If a person in a gorilla suit walked through a basketball game, would you notice?

Most people confidently answer yes.

But in a now classic experiment, roughly half of participants fail to notice the gorilla suit, when instructed to count basketball passes.

Participants were “instructed to count basketball passes,” thinking that was the primary assignment here. They were hyper-focused on the passes. If the participants were instructed to watch the court for any unusual object, it is not difficult to imagine them noticing a person with a gorilla suit.

Attention shapes how we experience reality.
Source: AI-Generated

The experiment demonstrated that we may experience the same reality in a very different way, depending on where we put our attention. In fact, this concept is probably not that novel. We experience it every day. When we are having a conversation, we usually tune out most of the other sounds in the environment.

We do not experience everything that enters our eyes and ears. We experience what receives attention.

This is because the brain receives vastly more information than consciousness can process.

Attention acts as a filter.

Without attention, consciousness would be overwhelmed.

Global workspace theory (GWT) holds attention as key to consciousness. Many specialized brain systems work simultaneously in the background. Attention is like a spotlight on a stage, which brings up small parts of brain processing into our awareness, where they become available to the rest of the brain.

Voluntary and Involuntary Aspects of Attention

Attention, just like many other brain functions, has parts that are under volitional control and parts that are beyond our control.

Biological constraints limit attention. We may forget or miss the gorilla because of resource issues.

At a basic science level, “attention blink” experiment reveals physiological limitation. Participants are asked to identify targets presented rapidly one after another. When the second target appears too soon after the first (roughly a few hundred milliseconds), people missed it—not because their eyes were closed, but because conscious processing was temporarily occupied.

In a broader everyday experience, we all know that we cannot fully control our attention.

Early in my career, I assumed that if I solved a patient's most bothersome symptom, they would feel dramatically better. Instead, I noticed something curious. Once one symptom improved, attention often shifted to the next problem.

This was not ingratitude. It reflected how attention works. The brain is designed to detect unresolved problems. What is fixed fades into the background. What remains broken captures attention.

Anxiety, cravings, anger, and rumination can all creep up and spiral. We tell ourselves we don't want to think about this anymore, yet we cannot stop.

On the other hand, in a condition like ADHD, patients have difficulty holding and attending to one thing or one thought. Their attention jumps from one thing to another.

You Become What You Attend To

But there are aspects of attention that are under volitional control. Attention is the currency of consciousness, and we need to make every effort to use this currency wisely.

The brain is constantly generating thoughts, emotions, memories, urges, and perceptions.

Most never reach awareness and remain unconscious, but those that repeatedly capture attention become our experience.

Over time, these experiences shape our identity.

In that sense, our lives are shaped by what we repeatedly attend to. Attention determines what enters consciousness, what is remembered, what is learned, and ultimately who we become.

You can choose what you attend to.
Source: AI-Generated

We cannot control everything that appears in the mind. But we can become more curious about what captures our attention—and more intentional about what we return to again and again.

Let’s start paying more attention to our attention.

item.title: How Childhood Emotional Neglect Can Affect Relationships
item.description:
Child Development

How Childhood Emotional Neglect Can Affect Relationships

Life after childhood emotional neglect: Why closeness feels difficult.

Posted June 8, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional disconnection can make relationships feel one-sided and unfulfilling.
  • You may give a great deal to others while struggling to share your own needs and feelings.
  • Feeling alone in relationships often comes from being disconnected from your own emotions.
Source: Ilona/StockAdobe

Growing up with your feelings ignored, childhood emotional neglect takes its toll on you. It’s true. In fact, it takes such a lasting toll that I can see its lingering effects decades later in my adult patients.

The Lingering Effects of Childhood Emotional Neglect

  • A lack of awareness of your own feelings, wishes, and needs.
  • A feeling that you are less important than everyone else.
  • A massive struggle to talk about and share your own feelings.
  • Difficulty asking for help and accepting help from others.
  • A lack of understanding of how feelings work in yourself and others.

Children who grow up with their feelings ignored take a very powerful step to get by in their childhood home. They wall off the deepest, most biological part of who they are: their emotions. That way, they can stop burdening others with their feelings. What a remarkable solution for a child’s brain to create.

But this solution does not come for free. As an adult, your life is greatly affected by it.

The lingering effects above are important parts of the toll of childhood emotional neglect. When your feelings are walled off, you are missing some life ingredients that will have a profound effect on your quality of life.

I know this because I see it in my therapy office every single day.

Whether you realize it or not, this group of struggles can affect many areas of your life. You are living without access to some vital ingredients of life that many others enjoy. It can make it hard to ask for a promotion or a raise, to trust yourself, or to take risks.

But there is one area of life that’s typically affected far more than any other: your relationships. As you read the five ways below, keep in mind that none of these are permanent. They are effects from your childhood, and you can fix every single one.

5 Important Ways Childhood Emotional Neglect Challenges Your Relationships

  1. It makes them one-sided. Generally, people with childhood emotional neglect are not able to be fully present in their relationships. When you’re not properly aware of your own feelings, wishes, and needs, how can you share them with a partner or friend? How can you take up your fair share of space in your relationships when you view other people and their needs as more important than your own? Many of your relationships become too much about the other person and not enough about you.
  2. Your relationships seem fewer and feel less rewarding than others’. Since you’re not fully emotionally present, your relationships may be limited in depth and resilience. They may break apart more easily or never reach their full potential. You may give a great deal, yet hold back the most valuable gift you can offer: your emotional vulnerability.
  3. It makes social time more tiring than it should be. Spending time with people you care about should be rewarding, energizing, and enriching. But you often find it draining instead. That’s because your relationships are one-sided, and also because you spend so much energy trying to be the person you think others want or expect you to be, instead of just being yourself.
  4. You feel alone, even with people who love you. All human connections are rooted in emotion. When your emotions are too blocked off, you may not have full access to that natural connection. Since you are unaware of the problem, you’re left feeling, on some level, emotionally isolated at key times. Even though you are actually not!
  5. It holds your relationships back from becoming as rich and deep as they should be. Just as emotion is the glue that binds you to others, it’s also the fire that lights your passion, and the stick that should be poking you, saying, “Speak up!” Without full access to this vital resource, your relationships are missing an important ingredient: You.

3 Answers Taken From the Book Running on Empty No More: Transform Your Relationships With Your Partner, Your Parents & Your Children

  1. Your emotional awareness: This involves being aware of what you are feeling and what the other person is feeling. It’s being able to observe your own behaviors and responses to things and understand the emotions involved.
  2. Emotion skills: Learning to identify what you feel, accept your feelings, tolerate your feelings, manage them, and put them into words. You can learn all of them.
  3. Communication skills: How do you tell someone they hurt your feelings? Or that you are angry at them? How do you ask someone for what you need or want? Once you get better at emotional awareness and emotion skills, you’ll have the foundation to learn how to communicate far more effectively.

Moving Forward in Your Relationships

As you read the challenges above, did you recognize yourself in one or more of them? Perhaps you saw how you give more than you receive, or that you hold back parts of yourself without even realizing it. Maybe you realized how you can feel alone, even when you’re not.

These are the natural results of growing up with childhood emotional neglect. You adapted in the best way you could, and that adaptation worked. But now, in your adult life, it may be holding you back from the kind of connection you want.

The most important thing to understand is this: what’s missing in your relationships is not your effort, your care, or your willingness to give. In fact, you likely have an abundance of all of those.

The only thing that’s actually missing is enough access to your own emotions.

Because it’s your feelings that connect you and guide you. They tell you when to speak up, when to reach out, when to set a boundary, and when to let someone in.

As you begin to turn your attention inward, to notice your feelings, to name them, and to accept them, something begins to shift. Your relationships can start to feel more balanced, more energizing, and more real, and little by little, you may find yourself bringing more of your true self into the moments that matter most.

A version of this post also appears on emotionalneglect.com.

© Jonice Webb, Ph.D.

item.title: A Neurodivergent Child's First Day of School
item.description:
Neurodiversity

A Neurodivergent Child's First Day of School

Starting school and neurodivergence: A fictional account through parents' eyes.

Posted June 8, 2026

Key points
  • The first day of school carries a different emotional weight for families of neurodiverse children.
  • Parents of neurodiverse children engage in extensive invisible labour, including preparation and advocacy.
  • Strong school–family relationships built on listening and openness create better outcomes for all.

Janet stood at the school gate on a warm morning with her 6‑year‑old son, Timmy. She stood surrounded by happy snaps, excited chatter, and parents comparing lunchboxes and uniforms. Everyone around her seemed upbeat with excitement and pride, celebrating their child’s epic milestone, the first day of school. Through her hopeful, misty eyes, Janet’s stomach churned with nerves. Pride, love, fear, determination, and exhaustion swirled together as she watched Timmy take those first steps through the school gate.

For many families, the first day of school feels like an epic milestone, buoyant with joy, celebration, lightness, and hope. For many families with neurodiverse children, like Janet’s, it arrives with a different weight, as if they are carrying the heavy baggage of past exclusions, stigma, and countless moments of feeling unheard. They carry this weight as the strong, seasoned advocates they are, parents who have spent years translating their child’s needs, navigating systems, and absorbing the emotional labour required to ensure their child is understood and supported, and protected from judgment and rejection.

The Role of Advocacy and Preparation for Neurodiverse Children

Janet joked with me that her parenting has made her an expert in what she calls “advertising.” She explained that advertising is her shorthand for the slow, thoughtful work of planting seeds, scaffolding tiny moments of success, and building familiarity. It is as much a strategy for getting through the week and weekend outings as it is a deliberate process of joining early‑years programs, walking past the school gate, pointing out classrooms, rehearsing routines, and creating micro‑experiences that help her child feel safe long before the first bell rings.

The night before school, Janet double‑checked visual supports, packed sensory tools, and mentally rehearsed the routines. Many autistic children experience differences in communication, sensory processing, and emotional regulation, and parents know that the smallest environmental mismatch can derail an entire day. As a single mum, Janet also carried the quiet hope that the day would go smoothly, that she would not be called away from work, that there would be no crisis requiring her to drop everything, and that the delicate balance she holds between caregiving and employment would remain intact.

Research shows that parents of autistic children are deeply involved in their child’s schooling journey, yet often have lower confidence in the school system’s ability to meet their child’s needs and report greater dissatisfaction with communication with schools. Australia’s National Autism Education Survey (2024) found that 45% of families report schools are reluctant to accommodate their child’s needs, 66% of autistic children experience bullying, 47% have changed schools at least once, and 43% refuse school weekly. These concerns weigh heavily on many parents’ shoulders. As Alexander (2024) found, “75% felt dismissed by school staff when raising concerns about their child’s needs.”

The Importance of Being Heard and Understood

On the other side of this experience, having a voice and feeling heard brings a sense of relief that soothes the inner storms carried by parents of neurodiverse children. This is what Janet quietly hoped for this year, a teacher who listens, stays open, and sees her child not as a problem to be managed but as a person to be understood. Parents like Janet are the historians of their child’s needs and the translators of their cues. They are seasoned advocates and interpreters who ensure those needs are understood by others.

So there she was, standing among the happy snaps and excited mums on a sunny morning of Timmy’s first day of school, carrying pride, love, uncertainty, fatigue, and hope. She lingered at the gate a moment longer, rolling up her sleeves for another year of advocacy, knowing that the first day of school marks the start of what she hopes will be a bidirectional and supportive relationship. She sent a quiet prayer for the other parents of neurodivergent children and for the hard‑working teachers who walk alongside them, all of them agents of change in their own way.

The first day of school is not just a milestone. It is the beginning of a relationship—a relationship that, at its best, is bidirectional, respectful, curious, and open to possibility. When communication flows early and often, when adjustments are offered with openness, and when families feel heard, the nervous system settles and trust grows. Research confirms that when schools and families work together with openness and respect, the best outcomes emerge, not only for neurodiverse children but for everyone. As in any meaningful relationship, the work is not in having all the answers but in staying curious, staying connected, and choosing again and again to meet each other with openness.
